# SCA driver fixtures — provenance

These files are **real output** from the exact scanner binaries pinned in
`integrations/scanner-image/Dockerfile`, run against the deliberately
vulnerable project generated by `../sca_fixture_project.py`:

| Directory | Tool | Binary verification |
|---|---|---|
| `trivy-0.70.0/` | Trivy 0.70.0 (`trivy fs --scanners vuln,misconfig,secret --format json`) | SHA-256 `8b4376d5…5aa9` (matches `TRIVY_SHA256`) |
| `osv-1.9.2/` | OSV-Scanner v1.9.2 (`osv-scanner --format json --recursive`) | SHA-256 `d6af4b67…b74b` (matches `OSV_SCANNER_SHA256`) |

Regenerate with `capture_sca_fixtures.py` whenever either version changes.

Notes on how they were captured (2026-10-15):

- The fixture project was written to `/workspace`, so paths match what the
  scanner container sees.
- OSV-Scanner ran with `--experimental-offline --experimental-download-offline-databases`
  because the capture environment's egress policy blocked `api.osv.dev`. The JSON
  schema is identical to online mode; only the advisory source differs.
  `osv-1.9.2/observed-api-failure.json` records the real exit code (129) and
  stderr produced in online mode when `api.osv.dev` was unreachable.
- `osv-1.9.2/cases.json` holds the real exit code, whether an output file was
  written, and the stderr tail for each edge case (clean, no manifests,
  malformed lockfile, the non-recursive `scan` subcommand).
- Size reductions only touch data the drivers never read: per-package advisory
  lists longer than 15 (Trivy) / 4 groups (OSV) are cut down (IDs the tests
  assert on are always kept, OSV `groups` are cut consistently), and OSV
  `affected[].versions` enumerations are removed. Every record that remains is
  verbatim.
- Trivy masks detected secrets itself (`****`); the fixture project's fake token
  is assembled at runtime and never appears in these files.

`sca-identity-vectors.json` is shared with the .NET test suite
(`ScaIdentityTests`) so the Python and C# identity normalizations cannot drift.
